opus-5.5.text:
I think it's quite hard, honestly, and the difficulty is mostly about our uncertainty rather than any technical limitation in writing questions.

The basic issue is that to get a benchmark that saturates smoothly, you need tasks spread across a wide and well-calibrated range of difficulty. You want some fraction the current models can barely do, some that are a bit beyond them, some well beyond, and so on, with roughly even spacing in terms of how much capability progress it takes to cross each band. But we don't have a good model of what "difficulty" means for AI systems. Human difficulty is a decent proxy sometimes, but it often breaks down. Things that are hard for humans, like recalling obscure facts or doing certain kinds of formal manipulation, can be easy for models. Things that are trivial for humans, like keeping track of a long-running task or acting sensibly in an unfamiliar environment, can be surprisingly hard.

So what tends to happen is that you build a benchmark thinking you have a nice spread, and then it turns out a large chunk of it hinges on a single underlying skill. Once models acquire that skill, a big block of the benchmark falls at once and you get a sudden jump. Or the opposite: a cluster of questions turns out to depend on something models are bad at, and progress stalls on them for a long time while everything else is already solved.

You can mitigate this somewhat. You can make the benchmark very diverse, so that no single capability dominates. You can use item response theory style approaches, where you estimate question difficulty from how existing models perform and try to fill gaps. You can keep the benchmark open-ended, with tasks that scale in difficulty along some natural axis, like the length or complexity of a task, so there isn't a hard ceiling. I think the task-length approach is one of the more promising ones, because it gives you a continuous dimension instead of a fixed set of items.

But even then, you're calibrating on the models you have today, and the next generation might have a qualitatively different capability profile. So I'd say you can do better than most benchmarks have historically done, but I'd be skeptical of anyone who claims they can design one that saturates at a genuinely even pace across several years of progress. The track record suggests our intuitions about what's going to be hard for AI are just not that reliable.

r001.rationale: The response explains that even a seemingly well-spread set of difficulty levels can still produce a sudden jump in scores when many questions depend on one underlying skill, so an even distribution does not ensure even-paced saturation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's quite hard, and I think the reason it's hard is actually pretty informative about what benchmarks are measuring in the first place.

So the thing you'd want, ideally, is a benchmark where performance goes from, say, 10% to 90% over a period of several years, and where the rate of progress on it tracks something like "how much more capable are the models getting" in a smooth way. The problem is that most benchmarks are constructed by picking a task distribution, and the difficulty of the tasks in that distribution tends to be clustered. Even if you try to make it span a wide range of difficulty, you're usually sampling from a fairly narrow slice of what's possible, because the people writing the questions have a particular level of expertise and a particular idea of what "hard" means. So what you end up with is a benchmark that sits at near-zero for a while, because the models are below the threshold where any of the tasks are doable, and then once they cross that threshold, a lot of the tasks become doable at once, and it saturates within a year or two. That's the pattern you've seen over and over: MMLU, GPQA, the math benchmarks, and so on.

If you wanted to avoid that, you'd need tasks whose difficulty is spread out over orders of magnitude in some meaningful sense. And I think the approach that's come closest to that is something like what METR has done with task length, where you ask how long a task takes a human expert, and you deliberately include tasks ranging from a few seconds to many hours. There, you actually do see a smoother trend, because the difficulty axis is continuous and spans a wide range. But even that has issues. The tasks at the long end are much more expensive to construct and evaluate, so you get fewer of them, and the measurement gets noisier exactly where you care about it most. And there's a question of whether "time it takes a human" is really the right difficulty axis, or just one that happens to be convenient.

The other problem is that even if you got the difficulty distribution right, progress on a benchmark isn't just a function of model capability. It's also a function of how much effort labs put into that specific thing. Once a benchmark becomes prominent, it starts to get targeted, either directly through training data contamination or indirectly through people building training environments that look like the benchmark. So you'd see progress accelerate on it for reasons that have nothing to do with general capability improving at an even pace.

So my honest answer is that I think you can do better than the current situation, mostly by being deliberate about spanning a wide range of difficulty and by using a difficulty measure that's grounded in something external, like human time or economic value. But I'd be surprised if anyone manages to design a single benchmark that saturates evenly over, say, a decade. I think the more realistic approach is to have a sequence of benchmarks and try to stitch them together, which is messy but probably unavoidable.

r001.rationale: The response says that even with the difficulty distribution right, benchmark progress also depends on targeted lab effort and contamination, so difficulty spread alone does not ensure even saturation.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s quite difficult, because you need to anticipate which capabilities are going to improve and how quickly. You can design a benchmark with a wide range of difficulty levels, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it will saturate at an even pace. Things that look very different in difficulty to us might all become easy for AI systems at roughly the same time.

For example, if a model is missing some capability that’s necessary for a whole class of questions, it might fail almost all of them. Once it acquires that capability, it could suddenly solve most of them. Spreading out the apparent difficulty of the questions doesn’t really protect you against that.

You could update the benchmark as models improve, adding harder problems to keep it informative. That seems more feasible, but then you have the problem of comparing scores over time. So I think you can design benchmarks that are more resistant to saturation, but getting a smooth, predictable rate of progress is a much stronger requirement.

r001.rationale: The response says that a wide range of question difficulties does not necessarily produce an even saturation pace.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s quite difficult, because you’d need to know in advance how capabilities are going to develop. You can make a benchmark with questions that span a wide range of difficulty, but that doesn’t mean performance will improve at a steady rate. Things that look very difficult today might become easy with one particular advance, while other things remain stubbornly hard.

And difficulty isn’t necessarily a single axis. Two systems can get the same overall score while solving quite different subsets of the questions. So even if you spread the questions out carefully according to what current models find difficult, that ordering might not hold for future models.

You could probably get something more gradual by making the benchmark very broad and updating it over time. But then you’re changing the measuring instrument, which makes comparisons harder. I’d be skeptical that you could design a fixed benchmark that reliably saturates at an even pace over a long period.

r001.rationale: The response says that spanning questions across a wide range of difficulty does not mean performance will improve at a steady rate, directly communicating that even difficulty coverage does not guarantee even-paced saturation.
